brief.title: Keep JSON store or move to SQLite?
brief.question: Should BenchMemo keep file-backed persistence for the next milestone, or move to SQLite now?

options.name: Keep file-backed persistence
options.description: Retain JSON-on-disk for the next milestone and focus on product workflow.

options.name: Move to SQLite now
options.description: Adopt SQLite before more product work to improve persistence durability.

constraints: Do not derail the next milestone

frame.normalizedQuestion: Should BenchMemo keep file-backed persistence for the next milestone, or move to SQLite now?

options.name: Keep file-backed persistence
options.description: Retain JSON-on-disk for the next milestone and focus on product workflow.

options.name: Move to SQLite now
options.description: Adopt SQLite before more product work to improve persistence durability.

constraints: Do not derail the next milestone

criteria.name: Risk
criteria.scoringGuidance: Prefer the option with the lower migration and rollback risk.

criteria.name: Velocity
criteria.scoringGuidance: Prefer the option that preserves delivery speed during the next milestone.

opt_file.summary: Keep the current store while product surface is still moving quickly.

claims.text: The current JSON store is good enough for the next milestone.
claims.rationale: It already supports the current workflow and avoids migration churn.

opt_sqlite.summary: Move now to avoid revisiting persistence later.

claims.text: SQLite would make persistence more durable immediately.
claims.rationale: A database-backed path could improve correctness and query flexibility.

opt_file.summary: Staying on JSON can hide future scaling problems.

claims.text: JSON persistence may become a bottleneck later.
claims.rationale: File-backed storage can become painful if concurrency or query needs expand.

opt_sqlite.summary: Migrating now costs time the milestone does not have.

claims.text: SQLite would introduce avoidable migration work right now.
claims.rationale: The repo already has a working store, so a migration would expand scope.

repoProbes.summary: The current JSON persistence is already isolated behind the file decision store and atomic writes.
operationalRisks: Longer-term concurrency concerns remain if multiple writers are introduced.

repoProbes.summary: Keeping the current store avoids a migration and preserves the current test surface.
Switching to SQLite would touch the store, data layout, and tests.
migrationHazards: Existing JSON data would need a migration path.

repoProbes.summary: SQLite adds migration and rollback work without solving a verified near-term pain.
migrationHazards: Migration correctness would need new tests and rollback handling.

evidenceItems.title: Current JSON store is isolated and already atomic
evidenceItems.excerpt: The current store already writes atomically and keeps persistence logic centralized.

evidenceItems.title: SQLite would expand the migration surface
evidenceItems.excerpt: A SQLite migration would change persistence format, tests, and rollback expectations.

claimStatuses.notes: Repo evidence supports keeping the current store for the short horizon.
The repo evidence shows migration work with no verified near-term payoff.
The current repo shape does not show an immediate concurrency or query crisis.
Migration work is real and near-term.

judgeDraft.executiveSummary: Keep file-backed persistence for the next milestone because the repo evidence shows the current store is already centralized and SQLite would add migration work without a verified near-term payoff.

criterionScores.rationale: Keeping the current store avoids an unnecessary migration and preserves the current rollback shape.
This option preserves milestone focus and avoids persistence churn.
SQLite could help eventually, but it introduces migration and rollback work immediately.
Adopting SQLite now would slow the next milestone.

keyRisks: JSON persistence should be revisited once multi-writer workflows appear.
dissent: If the roadmap suddenly requires transactions or richer queries, SQLite should move up.
nextSteps: Revisit persistence once the product needs exceed the current file-backed store.
